items.title: Stay Current with SAP SuccessFactors Performance and Goal Management: 2H 2026 Updates
items.author: jahnavia
items.text:
Hello SAP SuccessFactors Community! 
 The 2H 2026 release is here, bringing a solid set of updates across Goal Management, Performance Management, 360 Reviews, and Continuous Performance Management. Let's walk through what has changed. 
 Goal Management 
 1. Deprecation of Legacy Goal Management (Valid as of: November 12, 2027) 
 Legacy Goal Management reached End of Development on November 17, 2023, and End of Maintenance on May 17, 2024. It will be deleted on November 12, 2027. 
 The latest Goal Management has been available since 1H 2023, and SAP automatically upgraded all remaining customers when it rolled out universally in 1H 2025. A manual upgrade through Upgrade Center is still possible, but it cannot be undone, so review the differences first. 
 Action: Required. Future dates are subject to change. 
 Performance Management 
 1. Create Calibration Sessions from the Latest Team Overview (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Managers can now calibrate their team's ratings straight from the latest Team Overview. Selecting Start Calibration creates a calibration session for the employees, and if a session was already launched, the button opens the existing one. 

 2. Custom Manager Role Available in Route Maps for Performance Management and 360 Reviews (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 With Employee Central enabled, route map steps can now use the First Custom Manager role in the Manage Route Maps tool. This lets roles like Coach or Mentor take part in Performance Management and 360 Reviews. 
 First Custom Manager is the custom manager with the smallest Option ID in the jobRelType picklist. If several exist, only this one is used. 
 The role is available in the Modify, Signature, and Completion stages and in Single Role, Iterative and Collaboration steps. 
 It is supported in form assessment and routing, audit trail, reporting, Document Transfer, and Change Engine. 
 Document Transfer and Change Engine settings for the Custom Manager mirror those of the HR Representative. A new visibility setting hides a transferred form from the previous assignee, and it now works for Custom Managers and HR Representatives, not just Managers and Matrix Managers. 

 3. Enhancements to Business Rules in Performance Management (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Performance Management rule scenarios now support more conditions and outcomes: 
 Section Comments field: usable in the If and Then sections, just like Item Comments, and available for all form sections. 
 Length attribute: usable in the If section for Item Comments, Behavior Comments, Section Comments, and custom text or text area fields. The count excludes RTE-generated HTML tags. 
 Subject User fields: usable in the If section to base conditions on the form subject's Employee Central data, such as location, department, and job title. 
 Skill sections: behavior fields like Official Behavior Rating and Behavior Comment are no longer offered, since behaviors are not supported there. 
 4. Enhancements to the Latest Performance Management Form Experience (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Feature parity with the legacy form 
 Continuous Performance Management feedback is now visible on the form to any user who can access continuous feedback data for the employee, not just the employee, the manager, or the channel owner. 
 The Last Rating section now shows the rating source. With Job Profile Builder, a Rating Source field appears. With Talent Intelligence Hub, the label reads Last Proficiency Rating from Growth Portfolio, with a tooltip pointing to the Growth Portfolio. 

 Interaction patterns 
 Rating slider: the tooltip shows both the rating value and label, and the selected rating is displayed below the slider. 
 Long item names: names wrap across up to three lines, with a More/Less option beyond that. 
 Long button names: all names show in full in the confirmation dialog, and extra buttons collapse into the Additional Options (…) menu. 

 Send to {username}: when only one recipient is available in an iterative step, the button sits directly in the footer instead of the Send To menu. 

 Text changes 
 The words "skill" and "competency" are removed from button labels and messages, for exam,ple Remove and Are you sure you want to remove this item from the section? 
 The popover title in the Summary and Goal Competency Summary sections is now Breakdown of the {sectionName} Section . 
 The character countdown tooltip no longer uses technical terms like "tag" and "rich text". 
 Overall rating labels in the Goal Competency Summary section are clearer. Earlier, both goal and competency ratings were labeled Overall Form Rating, and the combined rating was labeled OCOC Rating. 
 Trailing colons are removed from labels such as Section Comments and Calculated Form Rating. 
 Message keys 
 The shared keys COMMON_Name, COMMON_Rating and COMMON_Description are replaced by form-specific keys, so these labels can be changed without affecting other areas 
 5. Expandable Custom Sections in Latest Performance Management Forms (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 A custom section can now be made more compact by showing its custom fields in an expandable side panel. In the main form, users see only the section title, description, and comment rows, and expand the panel to complete the custom fields. This option cannot be combined with Move this section under General Information . The result is less scrolling and a more focused review. 

 6. Form Launching Based on Permission Groups (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 In the Launch Forms tool, administrators can now pick a permission group under Select Employees to launch Performance Management and 360 Reviews forms only for members of that group who are also in their role-based permission target population. Only active employees are shown by default, and inactive ones can be included. Groups marked RBP-Only cannot be selected. 

 7. Form Template-Specific Ask for Feedback Emails (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Each Performance Management form template can now have its own Ask for Feedback email template. The notification type has also been renamed from Request Feedback Notification to Ask for Feedback Notification . When users select Ask for Feedback from Team Overview, the configured content appears as the default message, and they can edit it before sending. 
 8. Hide Action Links to Employees' Latest Performance Forms (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 The Performance Review action link to an employee's latest form can now be hidden in People Profile and on the Home Page, so users do not open forms that are not relevant to their review context. It is off by default and applies wherever the profile is reached, such as My Forms, the form header, the route map, or the Manage Team dialog on the Home Page. This came from customer idea 380249. 
 9. Hide Story Report Data for Performance Management Forms Never in Users' Inbox (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 A new Hide Story Report Data for Forms Never in Inbox permission, under User Permissions → Performance, works alongside Data Access: Story. Without it, users can see Story report data for forms that never reached their Inbox, including unrelated Ask for Feedback requests and responses. The permission is disabled by default. 
 10. New Rule Scenario: Configure Form Content Visibility in Snapshot Views (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Configure Dynamic Form Content applies only to forms in the Modify stage opened from the Inbox. The new scenario extends visibility control to snapshots: en-route, signature-stage, and completed forms, plus snapshots reached through audit trail, reporting tools, and Performance History in People Profile. 
 It works the same way as Configure Dynamic Form Content, so an existing rule can be copied and its scenario changed. The Current Step condition lets you vary visibility by step. 
 11. New Rule Scenario: Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Business rules can now send emails to specific users or teams when a form moves to the next step and meets defined conditions, which supports timely follow-ups like coaching or performance improvement plans. 
 Conditions: Employee Central data of the form subject, overall form ratings, custom fields, and other supported criteria. 
 Template built-in in Document Generation, with placeholders mapped to Employee Central fields, standard tokens, and custom form fields. 
 Recipients: internal users, external users, and distribution lists, including people outside the form route map. 
 Example use cases: notify Career Coaching when the manager's overall rating is below 3, notify Sales Performance when over 50% of a Sales employee's goals are rated Below Expectations, or notify Talent Management when Promotion Recommendation is selected. 
 12. Template-Specific Custom Labels for Latest Performance Management or 360 Reviews Forms (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Labels can now be customized per form template or section, and localized through Add More. This is based on customer idea 369330. 
 Custom Label for Attribute Type: replaces the default "Skill" or "Competency" in the rating table header, the Edit Weight dialog header, and the side panel item type indicator. The item picker keeps the default label. 
 Custom Label for "Name" Column and "Rating" Column: replace the default column titles in the Summary section. 
 In the Goal Competency Summary (OCOC) section, the label always stays "Competency", so exclude a relabeled competency section from the OCOC rating calculation to avoid confusion. 
 13. Text Improvements and Setting Removals in Performance Management Feature Settings Page (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Several labels and help texts were reworded. The key label changes are: 
 Previous labelCurrent label 

 Hide Delete Icon inside Form 
 Hide Delete Form button on forms 

 Rich text editor for PM and 360 
 Enable Rich Text Editor in the legacy form experience 

 Stack Ranker for Performance Management 
 Enable Stack Ranker for Performance Management 

 Enable the latest version of Stack Ranker for Performance Management 
 Enable the latest experience of Stack Ranker for Performance Management 

 Stack Ranker for Performance Management - Enable display of all forms but self 
 Allow managers to stack rank all reports 

 Enable the Objective Management-Performance Management Sync up 
 Enable auto-sync between form and goal plan 

 Enable user experience enhancements to Performance Management forms 
 Enable experience enhancements to legacy Performance Management forms 
 Two deprecated settings were removed: 
 Enable PM Form Search Competencies , because it applied to the deprecated Job Description Manager. 
 The rich text editor cleans up text pasted from Microsoft Word , because the cleanup now applies to both legacy and latest forms. 
 These changes apply whether or not the New Admin Experience switch is enabled. 
 14. More Features Available in the Latest Performance Management Experience in Mobile Apps (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 The latest mobile experience now supports: 
 Behaviors: view them without rating, rate behaviors instead of competencies, or rate both. Users can also add or remove behaviors, edit weights, and view rating gaps. This is based on customer idea 238731. 
 Attachments: users with the right permissions can add, view, and delete attachments on the form. 
 People Profile card links: links to User Information, Background Information, MDF Information, Development Goals, Performance Goals, Performance History, and Trend Information cards open from section descriptions. Block links from the legacy People Profile are not supported. 
 AI-assisted writing: covered in the next item. 
 15. AI-Assisted Writing Available in Latest Performance Management Forms in Mobile Apps (Valid as of: November 13, 2026) 
 Mobile users can now draft and refine comments with AI. 
 General actions (Enhance Writing, Make Short

items.title: System-1 decision models and tabular foundation models: who decides what in a business process
items.author: Phil_from_Madrid
items.text:
Enterprise workflows are weighed down by thousands of routine micro-decisions—routing a support ticket, verifying a supplier edit, or flagging an invoice for review. Rigid rule engines become brittle as edge cases multiply, while general-purpose LLMs are often too slow, expensive, and unconstrained for high-volume execution. 
 An emerging architecture suggests a more pragmatic division of labor: using fast, constrained classifiers for initial document triage, tabular foundation models to evaluate risk against historical records, and reserving slow reasoning—whether from an LLM or a human—for genuine exceptions. This article examines how this layered approach works in practice, the trade-offs between context and historical baseline data, and why vendor claims in this early space still require careful validation on your own numbers.

items.title: The Power of SAP Cloud ALM for Managing SAP Application Launch Projects
items.author: JohanPR
items.text:
What Is SAP Cloud ALM? 
 Before getting into the main topic, it is important to understand the functionality of SAP Cloud ALM. In simple terms, I define it as a command center that governs and monitors the performance and other relevant aspects of SAP solutions from a single place. 
 SAP has operated for many years as an umbrella of solutions, including applications such as SAP Ariba, SAP Datasphere, Concur, among others. Imagine the effort required to manage each solution from a separate portal to verify whether it is operating correctly in production. 
 A good analogy is to compare SAP Cloud ALM to an air traffic control tower: it allows you to know the route of the aircraft, their arrival and departure times, the altitude at which they are flying, and, when necessary, coordinate timely changes in direction to avoid setbacks. 
 Technical Definition 
 From a technical perspective, SAP Cloud ALM is a cloud-based solution for application lifecycle management. It enables organizations to implement, operate, and monitor SAP Cloud solutions with greater transparency, efficiency, and control.

items.author: AMIT_SHARMA01
items.text:
The Problem 
 If you're building a third-party integration either a mobile app, custom portal, or any external system that allows employees to request and cancel time off via SuccessFactors OData APIs, you may have run into this exact issue: 
 Employee cancels their time off request through your custom app. The EmployeeTime record correctly shows "approvalStatus = CANCELLED" in SF. But the manager still sees the request sitting in their approval inbox now showing a confusing "Cancelled" status that they can't do anything about, because the workflow instance itself was never terminated. 
 This is a common integration gap, and it happens because the business object and the workflow instance are two separate things in SF , and cancelling one does not automatically close the other. 
 This post demonstrates the full fix end-to-end, with real request/response payloads. 

 Why This Happens 

 Object What it represents What updating it does 
 EmployeeTime record The actual time off data (dates, type, status) Changes the record's own status field only 
 WfRequest (workflow instance) The routing object sitting in the approver's inbox Controls what the manager sees in their To-Do list 
 The EmployeeTime record and the WfRequest workflow instance are two separate objects in SF. Patching the record's approvalStatus field only changes the record itself it does not notify the workflow engine that the related approval item should close. 
 As a result, the workflow stays visible on the manager's screen even after the record shows CANCELLED , unless withdrawWfRequest is called explicitly to terminate that workflow instance. 

 The Full Flow: Demonstration 
 Step 1 - Employee cancels time off (existing working step) from Custom App 
 Below is the leave request detail Payload which be passed to CPI as request from custom application with Externalcode, User Id ( LeaveRequestID), Time Type, Start Date and End Date {
 "LeaveRequestID": "307eb8b817fd4e6c87f3d6ecdfc88cdf", --> External code of the leave
 "timeType": "1000",
 "userId": "test1",
 "startDate": "2026-10-01T00:00:00.000",
 "endDate": "2026-10-01T00:00:00.000"
} 
 Post Call: 

 At this point, the time record is updated but the workflow is still active on the manager's screen. This is the gap. 

 Step 2 - Retrieve the associated wfRequestId 
 Before you can withdraw anything, you need the workflow ID tied to this specific time record. Query it via the navigation property or a filtered lookup: 
 GET call: https://<api-server>/odata/v2/EmployeeTime?$select=externalCode,approvalStatus,endDate,startDate,timeType,userId,workflowRequestId&$filter=externalCode eq '${property.externalCode}' --> External code we got from mobile app ( in this case '307eb8b817fd4e6c87f3d6ecdfc88cdf') 

 Note: The exact navigation property name can differ depending on whether this is a standard object (EmployeeTime) or a custom MDF object . MDF objects typically expose this through a generic workflow association field configured in the object definition. Check your object's metadata ($metadata) if the property name above doesn't match your instance. 
 Step 3 - Withdraw the workflow (the actual fix) 
 Use the HTTP Adapter in CPI below screenshot to withdraw the workflow, 

 POST Call : 
 (use the worflow id from step 2) - https://<api-server>/odata/v2/withdrawWfRequest?wfRequestId=1937715L 
 API Response - 
 <d:WfRequestActionResponse>
 <d:element m:type="SFOData.WfRequestActionResponse">
<d:status>success</d:status>
<d:wfRequestId m:type="Edm.Int64">1937715L</d:wfRequestId>
 </d:element>
</d:WfRequestActionResponse> 
 The workflow instance is now terminated. It disappears from the manager's pending approvals, and the workflow history correctly reflects it as Withdrawn rather than leaving a dangling "Cancelled" item with no further action possible. 
 Pattern 
 Cancel object → Get wfRequestId → withdrawWfRequest (HTTP Adapter in CPI) 
 Applies to any standard or custom MDF object with workflow routing. 

 Error Handling: 
 Error Code Likely Cause 
 COE_GENERAL_BAD_REQUEST Either the API user lacks withdrawWfRequest permission in WorkflowAllowedActionList, or the wfRequestId is invalid/already closed 
 404 on the wfRequestId lookup The object may not have an active workflow (e.g., auto-approved request with no routing) — handle this gracefully and skip step 3 
 Permission error on withdraw Confirm this is a separate authorization from the one governing object creation/cancellation — easy to miss since the first two calls can work fine while this one fails 

 Summary 
 A clean cancellation flow for any workflow-routed object in SuccessFactors requires two actions, not one : 
 Update the business object's status 
 Explicitly withdraw the associated workflow instance via withdrawWfRequest 
 Skipping step 2 is what causes orphaned "Cancelled" items to linger on manager approval screens , a frustrating but entirely avoidable integration bug once you know the workflow engine and the business object are decoupled. 
 Hope you found this blog helpful, please leave your feedback or any suggestion in the comment. 
 Thanks, 
 Amit

items.title: SD Credit Management: 5-Level Approval Workflow for Credit-Blocked Sales Orders
items.author: Sneka_E
items.text:
In SAP Sales and Distribution, credit management helps control customer exposure by checking the customer's credit limit when a Sales Order is created. 
 In a customer implementation, I worked on a requirement where a Sales Order should still be saved when the credit limit is exceeded, but it should be credit blocked for delivery until the required business approval is completed. To address this, we implemented a 5-level workflow-based Credit Management approval process. 
 Business Requirement 
 Sales Order → Credit Check → Credit Block → Approval Workflow → Credit Block Release → Delivery 
 When the customer's credit exposure exceeded the available credit limit: 
 The Sales Order must be saved successfully. 
 The Sales Order must be placed under credit block. 
 A workflow must be triggered automatically. 
 The required approval level must be determined dynamically. 
 Approvals must be routed sequentially from L1 to L5. 
 After the final approval, the credit block must be automatically released. 
 If rejected, the Sales Order must remain blocked. 
 How the Approval Level Is Determined 
 The approval level was not fixed for every Sales Order. It was determined using: 
 Company Code + Credit Limit Exhausted Value 
 The Credit Limit Exhausted value was calculated as: 
 Credit Limit Exhausted = Sales Order Net Value − (Credit Limit − Credit Exposure) 
 For example: 
 Parameter Value 
 Credit Limit 1,000,000 
 Existing Credit Exposure 900,000 
 Sales Order Value 250,000 
 Available Credit 100,000 
 Credit Limit Exhausted 150,000 
 The calculated value is then compared with the customer's DoA (Delegation of Authority) matrix to determine the required approval level. 
 For example: 
 Credit Limit Exhausted Approval 
 0 – 25,000 L1 
 25,001 – 100,000 L2 
 100,001 – 250,000 L3 
 250,001 – 500,000 L4 
 > 500,000 L5 
 The above ranges are illustrative. Actual thresholds are maintained based on the customer's Finance/Credit Management DoA matrix. 
 Technical Approach 
 The workflow is triggered when the Sales Order is saved and the standard credit check results in a credit block. The implementation checks: 
 KNA1-KTOKD = 'XD01' 
 VBAK-CMGST = 'B' 
 The Sales Order number is then passed to the workflow. Before triggering a new workflow, the system checks whether an active workflow already exists for the same Sales Order. The required information is retrieved from SAP Credit Management and Sales Order data, including: 
 Sales Order Net Value VBAK-NETWR 
 Credit Control Area VBAK-KKBER 
 Credit Segment UKM_KKBER2SGM 
 Business Partner VBPA 
 Credit Limit UKMBP_CMS_SGM 
 Credit Exposure UKM_COMMTS_READ 
 The calculated Credit Limit Exhausted value is then used to determine the applicable approval level. 
 Approval Workflow 
 The approval follows a sequential process: 
 Sales Order 
 ↓ 
 Credit Limit Exceeded 
 ↓ 
 Credit Block 
 ↓ 
 Calculate Credit Limit Exhausted 
 ↓ 
 Determine DoA Level 
 ↓ 
 L1 → L2 → L3 → L4 → L5 Approvals 
 ↓ 
 Release Credit Block 
 ↓ 
 Delivery 
 Each approver receives the blocked Sales Order in the workflow inbox. If an approver rejects the request, the Sales Order remains blocked. The exact rejection and resubmission behaviour can be defined based on the customer's business process. After the final approval, the workflow automatically updates the credit status and releases the Sales Order from the credit block. 
 This implementation demonstrates how standard SAP Credit Management can be combined with SAP SD and workflow capabilities to handle credit-limit exceptions in a controlled manner. Instead of simply rejecting a Sales Order when the credit limit is exceeded, the order can be saved, credit blocked, routed through the appropriate approval hierarchy, and automatically released after the required approval. 
 This approach provides a flexible and traceable solution for customer-specific credit approval requirements in SAP S/4HANA. 
 Testing and Challenges Faced 
 During testing, one of the important things to check was whether the workflow was triggered only when the Sales Order was credit blocked. Since users can save the same order multiple times, we also had to consider the possibility of duplicate workflow instances being created for the same Sales Order. To avoid this, the system checks whether an active workflow already exists before triggering a new one. 
 Another scenario to consider was a change in the Sales Order after approval. For example, if the order value increases after the approval is completed, the previously approved amount may no longer be sufficient. In such cases, the credit limit exhausted value needs to be recalculated, and the approval level must be determined again if the change affects the approval requirement. 
 Partial deliveries also need attention. Even if a Sales Order has been approved, the system should continue to follow the configured credit-check rules for subsequent delivery processing. The workflow approval should not automatically bypass any further credit checks required by the business. 
 These scenarios highlighted the importance of checking not only whether the workflow works correctly, but also whether the credit status remains consistent throughout the Sales Order process. 
 What I Would Improve 
 One thing I would focus on is keeping the approval-level determination separate from the workflow logic. Since the approval level depends on the company code and the credit limit exhausted value, maintaining the DoA thresholds in a configurable table would make future changes easier. 
 I would also give more attention to Sales Order changes after approval. Recalculating the exhausted value before releasing the credit block helps ensure that the approval is still valid for the current order. This is particularly important when the order value or the customer's credit exposure changes while the workflow is in progress. 
 Conclusion 
 Implementing this requirement helped demonstrate how SAP Credit Management and SAP Business Workflow can work together to handle credit-limit exceptions. Instead of preventing users from saving a Sales Order when the credit limit is exceeded, the order can be saved and kept blocked until the required approval is completed. 
 The main advantage of the five-level approval process is that the approval authority is determined based on the actual credit limit exhausted value rather than following the same approval route for every order. Although this requires additional workflow logic and testing, it provides better control over credit exposure and supports the customer's DoA requirements. 
 Before implementing a similar solution, it is important to define the approval thresholds clearly and consider scenarios such as order changes, partial deliveries, rejection, and changes in credit exposure. These details help ensure that the credit block is released only when the required business conditions are satisfied.

items.title: Business AI in ABAP Cloud – A Strategic Overview (Part 1)
items.author: fabianfellhauer
items.text:
Business AI in ABAP Cloud – A Strategic Overview (Part 1) 
 Cheers ABAP folks! 
 If you've been anywhere near the SAP developer community recently, you've noticed that one topic keeps coming up in every conversation: AI . And with it, a question that many ABAP developers have been asking themselves — "Where does ABAP fit in an AI-driven world?" 
 The short answer: right at the center. 
 In the 2026 SAP Developer Insights Survey , ABAP remains the most widely used language in the SAP ecosystem at 82% . ABAP is not fading into the background. It is the technology backbone for SAP S/4HANA, SAP Integrated Business Planning, SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP Environment and with the ABAP Cloud development model, it is evolving to meet the demands of a cloud-native, AI-enabled future. 
 In this blog post, I want to give you a strategic overview of how Business AI capabilities are taking shape in ABAP Cloud: What's available today, what's on the roadmap, and how you can start building. 
 ABAP Cloud and AI — The Big Picture 
 Before we dive into the AI specifics, let's set the stage. ABAP Cloud supports a comprehensive set of development scenarios: From transactional SAP Fiori apps and embedded analytics, through process and data integration, to background processing and on-stack extensibility. The diagram below shows the full landscape, and you'll notice that Joule , SAP’s digital assistant, is explicitly part of the picture. Business AI is not a separate silo or an add-on. It is woven into the same architecture you already use for building ABAP Cloud applications with CDS entities and RAP Business Objects. 
 Figure 1: Joule integration in the ABAP Cloud development model 
 The Two Pillars: Embedded AI and Agentic AI 
 SAP's Business AI strategy in ABAP Cloud rests on two complementary pillars . The following diagram illustrates the overall strategy: 
 Figure 2: Business AI Strategy in ABAP Cloud 
 Embedded AI Capabilities in ABAP Cloud 
 Embedded AI refers to AI capabilities that run directly within your ABAP application . These are powered by the ABAP AI SDK , which provides the bare-metal functionalities, and the ABAP Cloud development model , which adds the integration, compliance, and UX layer on top. 
 Available and planned capabilities include: 
 Data Masking: Ensure privacy and compliance when sending data to AI models. Control what data leaves your system. 
 Document Extraction : Extract structured information from unstructured documents directly within your ABAP processes. 
 Document Grounding: Provide domain-specific context to AI models so that responses are accurate and relevant to your business data. 
 Data Prediction with RAP Recommendations : Leverage prediction capabilities integrated into the RAP programming model to suggest field values, next actions, or classifications. 
 Human-in-the-Loop with RAP Notifications : Keep humans in control. AI can propose, but users confirm with notification-based workflows built into RAP. 
 Background Processing Framework : Run AI workloads asynchronously using the Background Processing Framework (bgPF), so that long-running AI tasks don't block your users. 
 The key advantage of Embedded AI is the seamless in-app experience . Your end users don't need to learn a new tool or change their workflow — AI capabilities surface right where they already work. 
 Feel free to checkout the tutorial written by @jasmin_gruschke to jump start into the ABAP AI SDK. 

 Agentic AI Capabilities in SAP Business AI Platform 
 Agentic AI takes a different approach. Instead of embedding intelligence into a single application, it enables Joule and Agents to orchestrate across your business applications from the outside, through governed APIs . 
 The architecture supports: 
 Joule (broad-scope): SAP's digital assistant that can interact with your applications via natural language, performing the same tasks a user would. 
 Agents (narrow-scope): Specialised agents designed for specific, well-defined tasks with high automation potential. 
 Connectivity via OData, SQL, and MCP — Multiple integration paths ensure that Joule can reach your business logic regardless of how it's exposed. 
 Planned investments focus on ABAP side is on achieving unparalleled accuracy , generic API coverage across the application landscape, and enabling ECC environments , extending the reach of agentic AI beyond S/4HANA Cloud. 

 Ok, but when should I use what? 
 This is the question I get most often, and the honest answer is (like often in software development): it depends on the scenario , and in some cases, you'll want both. 
 Figure 3: Embedding AI vs. Agentic Orchestration 

 Embedded AI 
 Agentic AI via Joule 

 Development effort 
 Additional development required (ABAP AI SDK) 
 Remote service enablement required 

 Flexibility 
 Less flexible (model replacements, prompting bound to your code) 
 More flexible (orchestrated centrally) 

 User experience 
 Seamless, in-app, low entry barrier for end users 
 Natural language interaction via Joule, optimized via spaces concept in Joule Work. 

 Best for 
 Heavily used processes with high acceleration potential 
 Broad application coverage, high automation potential 
 My personal recommendation 
 If a process is used hundreds of times a day, every second counts and your active business users are used to an existing application: Embed AI directly into your application to see results fast. 
 If you want to enable your application landscape for AI-driven automation at scale, enable it for Joule . Be prepared to do this in the upcoming years for the most of your business processes. 

 Where can I find additional information? 
 If you would like to see an implementation of embedded AI in ABAP Cloud or the integration in Joule by using Joule capabilities in action, feel free to check out my recent Devtoberfest session on that. Watch it here : 

 Stay tuned for further blog posts, where we deep dive into the implementation details! 
 Cheerio ABAP Folks!

items.title: Lessons from SAP Ariba and S/4HANA Transformation Programs: From Requirements to Successful Delivery
items.author: Micky_Dange
items.text:
Having worked across SAP and enterprise technology transformation, I have found that successful delivery depends on more than selecting the right technology. Clear requirements, realistic dependencies, stakeholder alignment, integration readiness, and disciplined governance are equally important. 
 In SAP Ariba and S/4HANA programs, I believe teams should pay particular attention to: 

 Business process alignment: Validate procurement processes and business requirements before finalizing the solution design. 

 CRP preparation: Use Conference Room Pilots to validate realistic business scenarios and identify process gaps early. 

 Integration dependencies: Identify upstream and downstream dependencies across Ariba, S/4HANA, and integration platforms. 

 Testing strategy: Define end-to-end scenarios covering business processes, integrations, exceptions, and reconciliation. 

 Delivery governance: Maintain clear ownership of decisions, risks, issues, and cross-functional dependencies. 
 These practices can help teams identify problems earlier and improve the quality of implementation decisions. 
 I would be interested in hearing from fellow SAP practitioners: What has worked best for you in managing integration dependencies and business process validation during SAP Ariba implementations?

20.summary: The post asks whether a WHERE clause applied on top of a CDS table function is pushed down to the database tables or applied only after the SQLScript body has run. The author says they measured four styles of table function on S/4HANA 2023, using execution plans and timings. The excerpt contains only the question and the setup, with no plans, timings or conclusions, so the actual findings cannot be checked from this text.
key_points: Core question: does a consumer WHERE on a CDS table function reach the base tables, or is it applied after the full SQLScript runs?
The author compares four table function styles on S/4HANA 2023.
Method is stated as execution plans plus timings, but no numbers or plan excerpts appear in the excerpt.
The conclusion is not visible in the excerpt, so the answer to the headline question is unknown from this text.
technical_details: CDS table functions (AMDP/SQLScript-backed table functions in ABAP Core Data Services)
WHERE clause applied on the consuming CDS view or query
SAP HANA SQLScript execution and plan inspection
S/4HANA 2023 as the test release
20.why_it_matters: Whether filters are pushed down into a table function is a real performance question for CDS-based reporting. Wrong assumptions here can cause full-table processing inside SQLScript. The topic is relevant, but this excerpt does not yet provide evidence.
20.teaching_angle: Use it as a lab exercise: write a table function and a consuming CDS view with a WHERE, then compare the HANA execution plan (PlanViz or EXPLAIN PLAN) to see whether the predicate reaches the base table scan. Ask learners to predict the plan before they look, and to read the full post for the measured results.

7.summary: The post shows how to test SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 webhooks locally, without BTP. It treats External Hooks and Autoflow events as the same kind of mechanism, since both send HTTP calls to a URL you control. The author builds a local Python receiver exposed through ngrok, grows it from a single PreHook into a dispatcher that handles three mechanisms, and describes a self-inflicted deadlock and the fix that led to a threaded server. The excerpt has no code, so the implementation details cannot be checked from it.
key_points: External Hooks and Autoflow events are both outbound HTTP calls to a configured URL, so one local receiver can serve both.
A local Python receiver is exposed through ngrok, which avoids deploying to BTP during development.
The receiver starts with one PreHook and is extended into a dispatcher covering three mechanisms.
The author reports a real deadlock they caused, and the fix led to a threaded server design.
The deadlock details and final server code are not in the excerpt.
technical_details: SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 External Hooks (PreHook)
Autoflow events in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2
Local Python HTTP receiver with a dispatcher
ngrok tunnel to expose localhost to the cloud tenant
Threaded HTTP server as the final design
7.why_it_matters: Local webhook testing shortens the feedback loop for Cloud extensibility work. Learning that the two mechanisms are the same kind of outbound call is useful when reading the configuration screens. Practical deadlock write-ups in this area are uncommon.
7.teaching_angle: Good material for a hands-on session on extensibility: have participants build a minimal receiver that logs the payload of a PreHook, then extend it to route by event type. Use the deadlock story to discuss why a single-threaded receiver can block when the source system waits for a response.

13.teaching_angle: Use it in an architecture discussion on agent design: compare a single agent with context stuffing against a planner with a scratchpad and sub-agents. Ask participants what state each part should keep, and how the orchestrator should pass results back.

22.summary: The post explains an orphaned-workflow problem in SuccessFactors time off cancellation. Cancelling an EmployeeTime record through OData sets approvalStatus to CANCELLED, but the WfRequest workflow instance stays open in the manager's inbox. The fix is to read workflowRequestId and then call the withdrawWfRequest OData action from CPI, using the HTTP adapter. The post includes request and response examples and an error table, which makes it practically useful.
key_points: Updating EmployeeTime approvalStatus does not terminate the related WfRequest workflow instance.
The fix is a second call: read the workflow ID, then call withdrawWfRequest with wfRequestId.
The flow is run from SAP Cloud Integration using the HTTP adapter.
The error table separates permission problems (WorkflowAllowedActionList) from invalid or closed workflow IDs.
The post recommends checking $metadata when a custom MDF object exposes the workflow association differently.
technical_details: SuccessFactors OData v2 entity EmployeeTime with workflowRequestId and approvalStatus fields
GET /odata/v2/EmployeeTime with $select and $filter on externalCode
POST /odata/v2/withdrawWfRequest?wfRequestId=<id>
Response type WfRequestActionResponse with status and wfRequestId (Edm.Int64)
Error COE_GENERAL_BAD_REQUEST, linked to WorkflowAllowedActionList permission
SAP Cloud Integration HTTP adapter as the caller
The example uses wfRequestId=1937715L; the L suffix is OData literal notation and may not be valid in a plain URL query parameter, so check this before reuse
22.why_it_matters: Integrations that cancel time off without withdrawing the workflow leave stale approval items, which generates support tickets. The post identifies the decoupling clearly and gives a concrete, testable fix. Developers building SF integrations need this pattern.
22.developer_problem: Cancelling a time off request through the OData API updates the record but leaves the manager's workflow item open, so the manager sees a Cancelled item they cannot act on.
22.teaching_angle: A good integration exercise: have learners reproduce the cancel call, query workflowRequestId, and call withdrawWfRequest, then confirm the item leaves the inbox. Use the error table to discuss separate authorization for workflow actions, and ask learners how they would make the two-step call idempotent.

38.summary: The poster runs a Fiori Elements (OData V4, LROP) app generated in BAS against an ABAP environment trial, deployed via MTA to Cloud Foundry with a managed approuter and launched from SAP Build Work Zone. The BAS preview and the direct ABAP URL /sap/bc/ui5_ui5/... both work, but opening the app from Work Zone or HTML5 Applications fails: the $metadata request under /sap/opu/odata4/... returns 401 and a Basic auth popup appears. Re-entering client id and secret from a fresh service key changed nothing. The post ends with a question and contains no diagnosis or answer.
key_points: Route ^/sap/(.*)$ in xs-app.json forwards to a subaccount destination with authenticationType xsuaa.
The failing call is the OData V4 $metadata request, while the UI5 bootstrap works via direct URL.
The Basic auth popup suggests the request reaching ABAP has no usable user token from the approuter chain.
Refreshing destination credentials did not change the result, which points away from a simple credential typo.
The post does not show destination Check Connection output, the full xs-app.json, XSUAA scopes or role collections, or approuter logs.
technical_details: Managed approuter with html5 repo deployed via MTA to CF
Subaccount destination abap-cloud-default_abap-trial-<subaccount>, authentication OAuth2UserTokenExchange, generated by BAS
xs-app.json route ^/sap/(.*)$ with authenticationType xsuaa
ABAP environment instance default_abap-trial
Failing path pattern /sap/opu/odata4/sap/<binding>/srvd/sap/<service>/0001/$metadata
SAP Build Work Zone standard edition as launchpad
38.why_it_matters: It shows the usual gap between a working BAS preview or direct ABAP call and a CF-hosted app that depends on a token chain through approuter, destination and ABAP. Trial-specific setup makes it harder to reason from generic docs.
38.developer_problem: Why does a CF-hosted Fiori Elements OData V4 app on a managed approuter get 401 on $metadata against an ABAP trial, when it works from BAS and by direct URL?
38.teaching_angle: Walk the token path hop by hop: browser to approuter (XSUAA login), approuter to destination with user token exchange, destination to ABAP. Ask learners which hop drops the user token and what evidence (destination Check Connection, approuter logs, the user identity seen by ABAP) would prove it. Mark every candidate cause as a hypothesis to test, since the post itself gives no answer.

RAP Recommendations and RAP Notifications
Background Processing Framework (bgPF)

deep_dives.title: Testing predicate pushdown on CDS table functions
deep_dives.explanation:
Ref 20 asks the right performance question: when you put a WHERE on a CDS table function, does the filter reach the base tables, or does the whole SQLScript body run first? The author says they measured four table function styles on S/4HANA 2023 with execution plans and timings. The excerpt contains no plans, numbers or conclusion, so this briefing cannot tell you the answer. Read the full post before teaching any result.

What you can do now is set up the test yourself. A CDS table function is implemented by an AMDP method written in SQLScript. At runtime it is a HANA table function, and the consuming CDS view sends a SQL statement over it. Whether the optimizer can push the consumer's predicate through the function body depends on how the body is written. That is a hypothesis to test per style, not a rule.

A practical method: build the function over a large table, run the consumer with a selective WHERE on a key field, then inspect the plan in ADT or with PlanViz/EXPLAIN PLAN. Look at the rows produced by the base table scan and where the filter operator sits. Compare timings with and without the filter. Repeat for each body style, for example a plain SELECT, one that uses intermediate table variables, and one with parameters. Record the evidence, not the expectation.

A sensible shape is a root entity for the document, with one comment entity as child, rather than touching the standard tables. The comment table key would hold the document key (company code, document number, fiscal year), a line item number (set to a fixed value, e.g. 000, for header comments) and a comment sequence number. Whether BSEG should be your reference or a released CDS view over it is something to check in your release.

The count limits are business rules on the comment entity, so enforce them in a validation on save in the behavior implementation, not in the UI alone. The validation counts existing plus new rows per document and item and reports a message on the offending instance. Also consider a determination that assigns the next sequence number. Finally, a UI-side limit can be hinted, but only the validation is reliable because it also protects API and other callers.

interview_questions.question: A WHERE clause is applied on a CDS table function. How would you check whether it is pushed down to the base tables, and why can't you assume it is?
interview_questions.answer: A CDS table function is backed by an AMDP method in SQLScript, so HANA executes it as a table function and the consuming CDS view runs on top of it. Whether the consumer predicate reaches the base tables depends on how the body is written and on what the optimizer can do with it. I would not assume either way. I would build the function over a large table, query it with a selective filter, and open the plan in ADT or PlanViz or EXPLAIN PLAN. The things to check are the rows coming out of the base table scan and where the filter operator sits. I would also compare runtimes with and without the filter. Then I would repeat this for each body style, because the result may differ between them. Ref 20 describes exactly this kind of measurement, but its excerpt does not show the results.

interview_questions.question: Users must add at most 4 comments per FI document header and 2 per line item in a RAP app, stored in a Z table. How would you design it?
interview_questions.answer: I would not change BKPF or BSEG. I would create a comment table keyed by the document key (company code, document number, fiscal year), an item number (a fixed value for header comments) and a sequence number. In RAP I would model the document as root and comments as a child entity, or a standalone BO that references the document key, depending on how the standard data is exposed in the release. A determination would assign the next sequence number. The 4 and 2 limits belong in a validation on save, which counts existing and new rows per document and item and raises a message on the offending instance. UI hints alone are not enough, since other consumers could bypass them. I would also check the authorisation for the document.

interview_questions.question: A requirement says: error at save in ME21N and ME51N if a service number is duplicated across service lines. How do you find and validate the right enhancement point?
interview_questions.answer: First I would clarify the rule, because the request mixes a duplicate check with an empty external service number check. Then I would look for candidate BAdIs in SE18, such as ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST for PRs and ME_PROCESS_PO_CUST for POs, noting that these are candidates to verify in the release, not confirmed by the source. A where-used list on ESLL-EXTSRVNO and a debug session on save show what is called and whether service line data is accessible there. I would implement the check at save time only, so display mode is not affected, and issue an error message that stops the save. Then I would test the same rule in both PR and PO and in change mode, since a check in only one document can be bypassed.

top_stories.title: CDS table function pushdown: a measured test (findings not visible)
top_stories.summary: A blog asks whether a WHERE on a CDS table function reaches the base tables or is applied after the SQLScript runs. The author compares four styles on S/4HANA 2023 with plans and timings. The excerpt has no results.
top_stories.why_it_matters: Pushdown decides whether a table function scans the full table. Verify with your own plans before relying on any claim.

top_stories.title: RAP design: multiple capped comments on BKPF/BSEG documents
top_stories.summary: A forum post wants up to 4 comments per document header and 2 per BSEG line, in a custom Z table, with a List Report and Fiori app. Only requirements are given, no answer.
top_stories.why_it_matters: Key design and where to enforce the limits (validation) are the core RAP decisions here, and standard finance tables should not be modified.

top_stories.title: Fiori Elements V4 app returns 401 on $metadata via CF managed approuter
top_stories.summary: An app generated in BAS works in preview and by direct ABAP URL but gets 401 and a Basic auth popup on $metadata when opened from Work Zone. Refreshing destination credentials did not help. No diagnosis is given.
top_stories.why_it_matters: It is a token-chain problem across approuter, destination and ABAP. Check each hop with evidence.

top_stories.title: SuccessFactors orphaned workflow after time off cancellation
top_stories.summary: Cancelling EmployeeTime through OData leaves the WfRequest open. The fix reads workflowRequestId and calls withdrawWfRequest from CPI. The post has request/response examples and an error table.
top_stories.why_it_matters: It is the most concrete, testable fix today. Check the wfRequestId literal format before reuse.

top_stories.title: Save-time checks and migration fields in S/4HANA extensibility Q&A
top_stories.summary: Two unanswered questions: which BAdI validates service lines in ME51N/ME21N (ref 35), and how to add a custom field to the LTMOM Product migration object (ref 32).
top_stories.why_it_matters: Both show copied examples not matching the system. Confirm the available objects and hooks first.

top_stories.title: Business AI in ABAP Cloud: strategic overview, Part 1
top_stories.summary: Splits AI into embedded (ABAP AI SDK, RAP Recommendations/Notifications, bgPF) and agentic (Joule and Agents via OData, SQL, MCP). Some items are described as planned. No code or releases.
top_stories.why_it_matters: Useful for orientation only. Check availability per capability before planning.

top_stories.title: Integration questions: CPI lock conflicts and TPM Plain ID mismatch
top_stories.summary: Concurrent CPI updates fail with order locks (ref 40), and a TPM custom rule changes the Activity Plain ID so the PD lookup fails (refs 4, 47, a near-duplicate with a different suffix).
top_stories.why_it_matters: Per-key serialisation, retries and consistent lookup identifiers are recurring integration design issues.
